text: What is the shama and is it asserting
monotheism?
Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
the word shama can refer either to a
couple of verses within Deuteronomy 6
starting in verse 4 or it can be a
reference to a traditional Jewish prayer
that draws from these passages in
Deuteronomy 6 as well as passages from
Deuteronomy 11 and Numbers 15. But the
word shama is an imperative, a command.
It means listen or hear. And this is how
Deuteronomy 6:4 begins. In the Hebrew,
verse 4 says Israel, Adonai Elohu Adoni.
And when trying to interpret what's
going on here, Adoni Elohu means Adonai
our God or our God Adonai. It is using
an adjective to qualify Adonai. And then
the second part, Adonai, is a
predication. Adoni is one. So, it's a
clause, an X is Y clause. And there are
a few things to note about this in
relation to the widespread and
traditional view of Deuteronomy 6:4 as
the foundational Jewish declaration of
monotheism. The first is that the word
Elohu, which means our God, presupposes
the existence of other gods because it's
using the noun Elohim in the generic
sense of a deity, a god. Which god? the
one that pertains to us, the god of us,
not any other god. So it's presupposing
the existence of other gods. And it is
identifying Adonai as the one that
pertains to us. And then the second
part, Adonai, Adoni is one is not saying
there's only one God. It is saying
there's only one Adoni. And what exactly
does that mean? Well, this is debated.
There are some scholars who think that
this is a reference to monoyahism. So
Deuteronomy 6:4 would have been part of
the earliest layer of the original book
of Deuteronomy which was probably
composed under the reign of Josiah
toward the end of the 7th century BCE
where there would have been a number of
different cult sites dedicated to
Adonai. And so this might be a part of
Josiah's cult centralization,
centralization of worship in the temple
in Jerusalem. So rather than making
reference to the Adonai that is
manifested at Tamon or Shomrron, very
similar to the idea of the virgin of
Guadalupe or the virgin of some other
location. Maybe Deuteronomy 6:4 is
saying, "No, there's only one
manifestation of Adonai. Adonai is one
and it's the Adonai that manifests
themselves at the temple in Jerusalem."
So that is one theory of what's going on
here, but it's not asserting monotheism.
That is a post-biblical
theological and philosophical
innovation. But I think there's a better
reading of what's going on here. If we
look carefully at what it means to say
Adonai is one in the context of the
composition of Deuteronomy, what it most
likely means is Adonai is the only one
for you. In other words, it's demanding
an exclusive relationship, a relational
priority. And there are a couple of
different lines of evidence that
indicate this. To begin, Deuteronomy's
idea of covenantal love between Adoni
and the people of Israel is drawing from
the vassal treaties of the Neoasyrian
Empire and particularly those of
emperors like Srar Haden and Asher
Banipal which frequently demand an
exclusive love which is how it's talking
about dedication to the sovereign. The
vassels are subordinated to the
sovereign who is superior. And these
treaties frequently demand exclusive
love or exclusive dedication. And it
uses the language that we find in
Deuteronomy, including of the idea of
love. That's what we have in the very
next verse. Deuteronomy 6:5. You shall
love Adoni your God with all your heart,
with all your might, with all your soul.
And so it's drawing from these vassel
treaties that are all about saying, "I
am your superior. You are going to be
dedicated to me. You're not going to be
dedicated to anyone else." It's not an
assertion that no other empires exist or
no other sovereigns exist. It is a
demand that you be dedicated only to
this one sovereign. And there are other
passages in the Hebrew Bible that lend
further support to this interpretation
of what's going on in Deuteronomy 6:4.
For instance, in the Song of Songs, the
lover sings about his dove and his
perfect one and says she is a one. This
does not mean she's the only young woman
out there. In fact, this comes right
after a passage that talks about how he
doesn't care about all of the other
women that are out there. And so my
dove, my perfect one is one is an
assertion that she is the only one for
him, not the only one that exists. And
then the passage goes on to say she is
one to her mother,
the favorite one of the one who bore
her. And some folks might interpret this
as saying, oh, she's the only child of
her mother. But there are a lot of
scholars who suggest no. The fact that
she is identified as the favored one
indicates just that it's the same kind
of relational priority. She's her
favorite child. She is the one she cares
the most about. You are the only one for
me in the sense of you are my favorite
child. And so both of the clauses in
relation to the lover, in relation to
the mother support this interpretation
of identifying someone as ead in the
masculine or a in the feminine as one is
an assertion that they are the only one
for me, the only one I care about. They
are the preferred one. And so
Deuteronomy 6:4 in saying that Adoni is
one is saying Adoni is the only one for
you. This is exclusivity in
relationship, not in existence. It's
about a relational priority. And for a
wonderful discussion of the scholarship
and the history of the interpretation of
the Shama, I would recommend Nathan
McDonald's book Deuteronomy and the
meaning of monotheism, originally
published in 2003. There was a second
edition that was published about 10
years later. And chapter 2 is all about
the shama. And I want to point to the
summary of this chapter on page 95 in
the red box. The significance of the
shama Deuteronomy 6:4-9 is strongly
indicated by a number of factors
including its place in the structure of
Deuteronomy and its emphatic call for
wholehearted devotion. Its opening lines
make a declaration that Adonai is one.
As the following verse indicates, this
has personal and relational import.
Adonai is the only God for Israel. They
are to have no others. This may be
viewed as a positive restatement of the
first commandment. Both Deuteronomy 6:4
and the first commandment assume the
existence of other gods and that they
present a genuine temptation to Israel.
The Shama's relational claim on Israel
is further supported by consideration of
Deuteronomy 4:35 39 and 32:39.
The exact role of these verses in
Deuteronomy 4 and the Song of Moses has
not been fully explored. Instead, a more
limited task has been undertaken to
determine whether they excluded the
existence of other gods. Though some
have argued that they do, I have argued
that this is not necessarily the case.
And there are a lot of scholars who
agree with Nathan here, including for
instance Michael Heiser. And I have got
a paper that will be coming out in an
edited volume next year lending further
support to that argument. Rather, they
are best understood as making the same
sorts of claim upon Israel. the people
of Adoni as is found in the Shama. In
other words, that Adonai is the only one
for Israel. It's not saying Adonai is
the only God that exists. It is
demanding
this exclusive relationship. So, it is
not an assertion of monotheism. That
would be a post-biblical theological
innovation. It is a demand for an
exclusive relationship between the
sovereign and the vassel based on the
way the word ehad or akhat is used in
the Hebrew Bible based on the fact that
Deuteronomy is drawing from the vassal
treaties of the Neoasyrian Empire based
on the fact that the existence of other
gods is recognized from beginning to end
in the Hebrew Bible and is even
recognized in the New Testament as by
the way Nathan McDonald also discusses
in this chapter. of his book Deuteronomy
and the meaning of monotheism. So no,
the shama is not asserting monotheism.
It is demanding an exclusive
relationship between Adoni and the
